issues.failure_explanation: Removing previously selected points destroys compactness, so even a continuous exact error surrogate need not attain its next maximum. For example, take F={t e1+(1-t)e2/2: 0≤t≤1}, b=2, gamma=1, and r0(f)=||f||. The unique first maximizer is e1. On F\{e1}, the supremum of r0 is still 1 but is unattained, so the second selection is impossible. Moreover, sigma1=1/2, so this is not merely selection after convergence.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use approximate supremum selections when an exact remaining maximizer does not exist, and stop or pad a batch when its candidate set is exhausted. The source already permits arbitrary remaining batch members for the abstract analysis.
issues.overall_effect: The displayed algorithm is not executable for all compact sets covered by its formulation, even with an exact continuous surrogate. Finite-training-set implementations do not have this particular obstruction.
issues.title: The remaining batch maximizers need not exist
issues.why_classification: A selection-contract change is required on the advertised compact-set domain, but a contained replacement preserves the parallel batch method and its intended approximation framework.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: we actually do not need to fix how the remaining $b-1$ elements are chosen

issues.failure_explanation: Monotonicity of distance applies to a fixed vector, not to the comparison between f_n and the next batch's first vector. Take b=2, gamma=1, F={e0, 0.9e0+0.1e1, 0.5e2}, and the exact surrogate. The first batch selects the first two vectors. Then |a11|=0.1 while sigma2=0.5, contradicting P1. All three vectors are independent, so the failure is not a degenerate Gram–Schmidt example. Stale-ranked batch members can also be exactly dependent, exposing the same lack of a positive-pivot guarantee in the indexed basis setup.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must replace the false pointwise residual bound with valid batch-level control, handle dependent batch members, and redo the product and rate arguments. Enforcing weak-greedy residual selection after every insertion would instead abandon the stated parallel preselection mechanism.
issues.overall_effect: The central determinant lower bound and the ensuing Hilbert and Banach convergence estimates are unsupported for the stated batch selection. In particular, the advertised batch-size-independent asymptotic loss is not established.
issues.title: Stale batch scores do not imply the asserted diagonal lower bound
issues.why_classification: The supporting lemma is false for legitimate executions. Repairing the analysis requires a new batch-level argument or a substantial change to the selection guarantee and potentially to the claimed dependence of the convergence rate on batch size.

issues.failure_explanation: Taking the 2n-th root gives exponent (n-m)/n, not (n-m)/m. The stronger stated estimate is false independently of batching: with b=gamma=1 and F={delta e1,...,delta e4}, strong greedy has sigma3=delta and d1≤delta. The stated m=1 bound would give delta≤sqrt(2)delta², which fails for delta=1/4.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the exponent (n-m)/m by (n-m)/n, retaining the square-root special case actually supported by the calculation.
issues.overall_effect: The general comparison in part (i) is materially stronger than its proof and is false even for the classical strong greedy algorithm. The separately stated square-root special case uses the correct exponent.
issues.title: The Hilbert width comparison claims the wrong power of d_m
issues.why_classification: The source supplies a comparable corrected estimate, but the repair withdraws a substantively stronger power-law comparison rather than merely correcting notation.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: their values improve ($C_1(n,\hue{b})$ decreases and $c_1(n,\hue{b})$ increases) for increasing $n$

issues.failure_explanation: The case split writes M=ceil(c+(b-1)/s)s+q, so its required constant involves the smaller auxiliary index s. The theorem instead evaluates the ceiling at the output index M. Since these ceilings decrease with their argument, the final inequalities do not contradict the stated constants. For example, in part (iii), b=30, M=31, s=1 gives ceiling 31 in the proof but ceiling 3 in the theorem. The same substitution is repeated in the Banach rate proofs. It remains invalid even if the product estimates are granted.

failure_location.quote: This yields the desired contradiction $C_1 < 2^{\alpha + 1} \gamma^{-2} \left\lceil 4 + \frac{\hue{b-1}}{s}\right\rceil^{2\alpha} C_0$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Carry the actual auxiliary index through the estimates. For exponential bounds, use s=floor((n-b+1)/2) directly in the established shifted estimate. For polynomial bounds, use a genuinely uniform induction constant, with ceiling bounds uniform in s, and revise the finite-prefix and corollary statements accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: The explicit n- and b-dependent polynomial and exponential constants, their claimed onset after the first batch, and the derived loss comparison are not proved by these contradiction arguments.
issues.title: Rate constants are evaluated at the output index instead of the auxiliary index
issues.why_classification: A contained reindexing and constant recalculation can retain polynomial and exponential convergence forms, but the advertised explicit constants and their range cannot be preserved by the written argument.

issues.failure_explanation: The comparison for M≤b requires c1≥0. However, the hypotheses permit 0<C0<gamma²/2, giving C1<1 and hence c1=ln(C1)b^(-alpha)<0. For M<b, C1 exp(-c1 M^alpha)=C1^(1-(M/b)^alpha)<1, whereas its value at b is 1; the displayed inequality is reversed. Thus the normalization sigma0≤1 does not supply the claimed contradiction, and the stated c1 is not a positive decay coefficient in this regime.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Treat C1≤1 separately, or explicitly enlarge C0 to max(C0,1) before defining the exponential constants. This preserves the width hypothesis and makes the base-case monotonicity and positive decay coefficient valid.
issues.overall_effect: The finite-prefix proof of part (iii) does not cover all permitted width constants, separately from the batch-index conversion error.
issues.title: The Hilbert exponential base case assumes an unstated sign condition
issues.why_classification: A local normalization or short additional base-case argument preserves the approximation regime and exponential convergence form without changing the proof architecture.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof substitutes the uncapped first branches without establishing that they apply. With alpha=c0=C0=gamma=1 and n=b=100, C1=sqrt(2), the stated constants give c1(n,1)=1/8 and c1(n,b)=ln(sqrt(2))/100, not (2/3)(1/8)=1/12. The immediately preceding piecewise reformulation also uses the logarithmic branch at n=b, which the corollary explicitly includes.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State the comparison only for explicitly defined uncapped large-index constants and their valid range, retaining capped estimates elsewhere. If the comparison is to hold with one coefficient throughout the claimed range, enlarge the prefactor in a b-dependent way so both logarithmic caps are inactive.
issues.overall_effect: The asserted universal coefficient identity does not follow from either the minimum-defined constants or the included base-case branch. This defect is separate from whether the underlying rate estimates are valid.
issues.title: The loss identity drops the logarithmic branches of the rate constants
issues.why_classification: The fixed quantitative comparison requires a restricted range or a changed prefactor. A comparable asymptotic comparison can survive without new global proof architecture, but not with the constants and range currently asserted.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: If the infimum in the definition of $d_n$ is attained, the corresponding argument $X_n$ is called \emph{optimal in the sense of Kolmogorov}.

issues.failure_explanation: For an arbitrary Banach space, the definition of d_m as an infimum does not supply an optimal subspace. The source explicitly makes attainment conditional, but this proof assumes it without an attainment hypothesis or argument. The subsequent vectors h_i and the approximation bound by exactly d_m rely on that unsupported choice.

failure_location.quote: Let $X_m$ be an $m$-dimensional optimal subspace of $X$ in the sense of Kolmogorov, i.e., $\dist(\cF,X_m)=d_m$, $m=1,\ldots, K$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Choose an epsilon-optimal m-dimensional subspace, carry d_m+epsilon through the estimates, and let epsilon decrease to zero.
issues.overall_effect: The product proof does not cover the full stated Banach-space scope as written.
issues.title: The Banach product proof assumes attainment of the Kolmogorov width
issues.why_classification: The epsilon-optimal-subspace bypass is local and preserves the product inequality, all constants, and the full Banach-space scope.

issues.failure_explanation: Put p=alpha-beta-1/2>0 and A=ceil(2+(b-1)/4). The base-case argument needs C1≥(4A-1)^p, but the displayed second term is only 4(A-1)^p. These are not interchangeable. For b=1, alpha=7/4, beta=1/4, gamma=1, and sufficiently small C0, the stated maximum equals 4. At the allowed base index M=7, its alleged lower bound is then 4/7<1. This failure already occurs when the batch-dependent ceiling mismatch is absent.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the second term in C1 by (4 ceil(2+(b-1)/4)-1)^(alpha-beta-1/2), or a larger valid base-case constant.
issues.overall_effect: The contradiction proof does not establish the polynomial estimate over its initial index range with the stated normalization.
issues.title: The Banach polynomial base-case constant does not imply the claimed bound
issues.why_classification: This is a routine local base-case normalization change; the polynomial exponent, parameter regime, and induction architecture remain unchanged.

issues.failure_explanation: The function sqrt(t) exp(-c t^alpha) is not generally decreasing, so controlling its value at b does not control all earlier indices; Case 2 also makes an unjustified comparison of this function at different indices. The theorem itself fails in the base range: in l_infinity take F={(1,0,...),(1,1,0,...)}, gamma=1, b=2, and choose the first vector first. Then sigma1=1, while d1≤1/3 using span{(1,1/2,0,...)} and d_n=0 for n≥2. Set alpha=1, C0=1/2, c0=ln(3/2). All width hypotheses hold, but C1=1 and c1(1,2)=c0/12>0, so the asserted bound gives sigma1≤exp(-c0/12)<1.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Control the finite prefix explicitly, for example by enlarging C1 above 1 and using a cap no larger than ln(C1)b^(-alpha). In the large-index argument, compare the square-root prefactors directly and then compare exponents, rather than assuming the whole prefactor-weighted exponential is decreasing.
issues.overall_effect: Part (iii) is false for legitimate inputs, independently of the diagonal-bound and auxiliary-index defects. Its intermediate-index argument also lacks a valid monotonicity justification.
issues.title: The Banach exponential proof incorrectly assumes monotonicity of its prefactor-weighted exponential
issues.why_classification: A contained reworking of the prefactor and base-case constants can retain the square-root-times-exponential convergence form and full parameter scope, but the current quantitative bound must be weakened.
